extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112) and whether required experimentation would be 'undue.' Directed primarily to examiners conducting enablement rejections and to applicants responding with evidence or argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement test
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of enablement is whether one reasonably skilled in the art could make or use the invention from the disclosures in the patent coupled with information known in the art without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent need not teach what is well known in the art and may omit such material. Determination of enablement is a question of law based on underlying factual findings. (Cites: In re Wands; United States v. Telectronics; In re Buchner; Hybritech; etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Undue experimentation factors (Wands factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many factors to be considered when determining whether necessary experimentation is 'undue.' These factors include, but are not limited to: (A) the breadth of the claims; (B) the nature of the invention; (C) the state of the prior art; (D) the level of one of ordinary skill; (E) the level of predictability in the art; (F) the amount of direction provided by the inventor; (G) the existence of working examples; and (H) the quantity of experimentation needed to make or use the invention based on the content of the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a single factor to conclude nonenablement; weigh all factors and the evidence as a whole. Examiner must consider all evidence related to each factor and base any conclusion of nonenablement on the record as a whole. (Cites: In re Wands.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth vs enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must teach how to make and/or use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation; if it does not, enablement is lacking for the full scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making an enablement rejection, explain why the scope of protection sought is not adequately enabled and provide specific findings of fact (e.g., missing information about essential parts or relationships). Identify information missing and why one skilled in the art could not supply it without undue experimentation. References should be supplied if possible to support a prima facie case. (See MPEP § 2164.06(a), In re Marzocchi.)

rubrics_metrics.name: How to make the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as the specification discloses at least one method for making and using the claimed invention that bears a reasonable correlation to the entire scope of the claim, the enablement requirement is satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose other methods does not render a claim invalid. For unstable/transitory intermediates, teaching how to make non-stable isolatable forms is not required. If practice of the method requires particular apparatus or chemicals not readily available, the application must sufficiently disclose them. (Cites: In re Fisher; In re Breslow; In re Ghiron; In re Howarth.)

rubrics_metrics.name: How to use the claimed invention (utility/use limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a statement of utility contains a connotation of how to use, or standard modes of administration are known and contemplated, 35 U.S.C. 112 is satisfied for 'how to use.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dosage or method need not be specified if one skilled in the art could obtain such information without undue experimentation based on knowledge of similar compounds. If claim is limited by a particular use, evaluate enablement based on that limitation. If claim is not limited by a use, any enabled use reasonably correlating with the entire scope is sufficient to preclude a nonenablement rejection. If multiple uses are disclosed, an enablement rejection must explain why the specification fails to enable each disclosed use. (Cites: In re Johnson; In re Hitchings; In re Brana; In re Vaeck.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Working examples (presence and weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with enablement does not hinge on disclosure of examples; examples may be 'working' (based on actual work) or 'prophetic.' The specification need not contain an example if the invention is otherwise disclosed enablingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of working examples is a factor to consider, especially in unpredictable/undeveloped arts, but absence should never be the sole reason for rejecting on enablement grounds. A single working example can preclude a rejection that nothing is enabled, but presence of only one example is not by itself a reason to reject claims as broader than the enabling disclosure. Examiner must evaluate whether extrapolation from the one example across the claim scope is reasonable and explain why not if rejecting. (Cites: Gould v. Quigg; In re Borkowski; In re Wands.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of in vitro / in vivo examples
rubrics_metrics.description: An in vitro or in vivo animal model example in the specification constitutes a 'working example' only if it 'correlates' with the disclosed or claimed method of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the art recognizes a model as correlating to a specific condition, it should be accepted unless examiner has evidence it does not correlate. Examiner carries initial burden to give reasons for lack of correlation and must weigh evidence for and against correlation; rigorous exact correlation is not required. (Cites: In re Brana; Cross v. Iizuka.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Working examples and claimed genus
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claimed genus, representative examples together with a statement applicable to the genus as a whole will ordinarily be sufficient if one skilled in the art would expect the genus could be used without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement for other members of the genus is required only where examiner advances adequate reasons showing a skilled person could not use the genus as a whole without undue experimentation. Examiner must provide such reasons supported by evidence. (See MPEP discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability of the art (relationship to required disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of guidance needed to enable the invention is inversely related to knowledge in the prior art and predictability in the art: the more predictable the art, the less explicit information needed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nascent or unpredictable technologies require more specific and useful teaching. In unpredictable arts (e.g., many chemical and physiological activities), disclosure of a single species usually does not support broad genus claims; in predictable arts (mechanical, electrical), a single embodiment may provide broad enablement. (Cites: In re Fisher; In re Vickers; In re Soll; Chiron v. Genentech.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the examiner to support nonenablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Before enabling analysis, examiner must construe the claims. The examiner has the initial burden to establish a reasonable basis to question the enablement provided for the claimed invention and must provide a reasonable explanation why the scope is not adequately enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must set forth claim meanings when terms are ambiguous. To make a rejection, the examiner must explain why the examiner doubts the truth/accuracy of any supporting disclosure and back up assertions with acceptable evidence or reasoning. Minimal requirement per In re Bowen: give reasons explaining uncertainty. Specific technical reasons are always required. Examiner should not base determination on one factor alone and must consider all evidence related to Wands factors. (Cites: Genentech v. Wellcome; In re Wright; In re Marzocchi; In re Bowen; In re Wands.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of enablement based on the evidence as a whole (applicant rebuttal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once examiner establishes a reasonable basis to question enablement, the burden falls on applicant to present persuasive arguments and suitable proofs showing one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the application as a guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may submit affidavits/declarations (37 CFR 1.132) or cite references. Declarations are evidence whose weight depends on supporting factual detail; conclusory expert statements are insufficient. Examiner must compare conditions in post-filing declarations with the disclosure to ensure commensurate scope. Examiner must weigh all evidence (specification, applicant's new evidence, references/evidence in rejection) and decide based on the weight of the record, not personal opinion. (Cites: In re Brandstadter; In re Buchner; In re Alton; Scott v. Finney.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification enabling as of the filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification is enabling must be assessed as of the filing date, considering the nature of the invention, the state of the prior art, and the level of skill in the art at that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state of the prior art at the filing date is used to determine enablement; later publications generally cannot be used to show what was known at filing, with limited exceptions where later references demonstrate what skilled artisans would have known earlier. The specification need not disclose what is well-known to those skilled in the art. The pertinent art should be defined in terms of the problem to be solved. (Cites: Chiron v. Genentech; In re Gunn; In re Budnick; In re Wright.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable persons skilled in the relevant arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable a person 'skilled in the art to which it pertains' (or most nearly connected), and when different arts are involved, the disclosure is enabling if persons skilled in each relevant art can practice the aspect applicable to their specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple distinct technologies are relevant, the disclosure is adequate if a person of ordinary skill in each technology could practice the invention from the disclosure (e.g., cooperation between specialists). (Cites: In re Naquin; Technicon Instruments v. Alpkem; Ex parte Zechnall.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of experimentation (qualitative not merely quantitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of experimentation needed is one factor in deciding undue experimentation; the test is not merely quantitative because considerable experimentation may be permissible if it is routine or the specification gives reasonable guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time and expense are factors but not controlling. Examples: Telectronics — $50,000 and 6–12 months did not show undue experimentation where guidance and an embodiment were provided; In re Ghiron — functional block diagrams and lack of detail that required months/years of development supported nonenablement. Examiner should consider whether experimentation is routine and whether the specification directs the direction of experimentation. (Cites: In re Colianni; In re Wands; US v. Telectronics; In re Ghiron.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction prior to enablement analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Before any enablement analysis, the examiner must construe the claims and, for ambiguous terms, select the definition intended for examination and explicitly set forth the meaning and scope in an Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction sets the scope against which enablement is judged. For terms not well-known or having multiple meanings, the examiner's stated construction guides the enablement analysis and the rejection. (Cites: Genentech v. Wellcome.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution / best-first Office action practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In accordance with compact prosecution, if an enablement rejection is appropriate the first Office action on the merits should present the best case with all relevant reasons, issues, and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the best rejection early so applicant can rebut; identify limitations that would render claims enabled and communicate enabled, allowable subject matter to applicant as early as possible. This helps allow subsequent Office actions to be final if applicant fails to rebut. Avoid expanding arguments in later Office actions unnecessarily. (Policy guidance in MPEP.)
